pos: n. (Hendrik de Cock, 1801–1842, minister at Ulrum in Groningen, deposed in 1834 and father of the Dutch Secession)
etymology: Dutch Hendrik, from Germanic haim, home, and ric, ruler; de Cock, the cook.
biblical_def: Hendrik de Cock was trained in the rationalist theology of Groningen and came to Ulrum in 1829 as a conventional minister of the Netherlands Reformed Church. His conversion came through his own parishioners and through old books: a labourer named Klaas Kuipenga asked him whether he could add even one sigh to his own salvation, and De Cock, reading Calvin's Institutes and the Canons of Dort for the first time, found the doctrine of grace his church still confessed on paper and denied in its pulpits. Earnest believers began to come to Ulrum from neighbouring parishes to hear him and to have their children baptized. In 1833 he wrote against two ministers he called wolves in the flock and prefaced a pamphlet attacking the church's imposed hymnbook; the classis suspended him, and in 1834 the synod deposed him. On 13 October 1834 the consistory and congregation of Ulrum signed the Act of Secession or Return, withdrawing from the state-organized church and returning to the confessions and the church order of Dort. De Cock was fined and imprisoned for three months, and soldiers were quartered on his people. He died at forty. His text was Jeremiah's: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deposition in church law as the depriving of a clergyman of his orders.
webster_full: DEPOSI'TION, n. The act of dethroning a king, or the degrading of a person from an office or station; a divesting of sovereignty, or of office and dignity.
SECES'SION, n. The act of withdrawing, particularly from fellowship and communion.
CONSIS'TORY, n. An assembly of ministers and elders; the court of a church.
scriptures: Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
corruption_summary: A Groningen rationalist converted by a farmhand's question, and deposed for preaching the church's own confession.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption De Cock exposed is the one that empties a confessional church without amending a word of its confession: ministers who subscribe the Three Forms of Unity only insofar as they agree with Scripture, rather than because they do. By 1834 the Netherlands Reformed Church punished a man for preaching the Canons of Dort while it tolerated ministers who openly denied them. When a church disciplines fidelity and protects unbelief, the word of Peter governs: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

The second corruption is the one his enemies charged against him, that secession is schism. De Cock did not found a new church; the Act of 1834 was an act of return, and he called it so. The modern habit of treating every departure from a declining denomination as divisiveness forgets that the call of 2Co 6:17 is also a word of the Lord: “come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17).
roots_summary: Hebrew olam (H5769), antiquity; nathiyb (H5410), path; Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, set apart; 2 Corinthians 6:17.
usage: “ask for the old paths” (Jer 6:16) — the Secession as return.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — his answer to the synod.
“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — the prisoner of 1835.

pos: n. (Helenius de Cock, 1824–1894, son of Hendrik de Cock, minister and professor at the Theological School at Kampen)
etymology: Latinized Greek Helenius, from helene, a torch; de Cock, the cook.
biblical_def: Helenius de Cock was ten years old when his father was deposed and the congregation of Ulrum seceded, and he grew up in a persecuted church. He studied for the ministry under the Seceder pastors who trained men in their own homes before the churches had a school, served congregations in the Christian Seceded Reformed Church, and in 1854 became one of the first teachers of the Theological School at Kampen, where he taught for the rest of his working life. His loyalty was to the confessional and Dortian character of the Secession against both the national church it had left and the newer movement under Abraham Kuyper that it would join in 1892. Late in life he wrote the biography of his father, preserving the documents and memories of 1834 for a generation that had not suffered for them. He is an example of the second generation's calling, to hand on what the first generation recovered: “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). His office was Paul's charge to Timothy, “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a professor as one who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning, and biography as the history of the life of a particular person.
webster_full: PROFES'SOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university, college or other seminary.
BIOG'RAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.

POL'ITY, n. The form or constitution of the civil government of a nation or state; or the general fundamental principles of that form of government. Ecclesiastical polity, the government of the church.
scriptures: Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The son of the Secession, who taught the next generation what their fathers had suffered for.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger his life addresses is the ordinary one of the second generation, which inherits a costly recovery as a settled custom and soon cannot say why the fathers left. Psa 78:4 makes the transmission a duty, not a sentiment: “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4).

The principle to recover is that church history and church polity are not antiquarian subjects but means of fidelity. A minister must be “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9), and a seminary that forgets how its church came to exist will not long remember what it believes.
roots_summary: Hebrew dor (H1755), generation; Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit; pistos (G4103), faithful.
usage: “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4) — the biographer's duty.
“commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the professor's office.
“the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — why a church keeps a school.

pos: n. (Simon van Velzen, 1809–1896, leader of the Dutch Secession of 1834 and professor at Kampen)
etymology: Hebrew Shimon, hearing; Dutch van Velzen, of Velsen, a village in North Holland.
biblical_def: Simon van Velzen belonged to the Leiden student circle known as the Scholte club, together with Hendrik Scholte, Anthony Brummelkamp, and Albertus van Raalte, and he joined the Secession at its beginning, when he was minister at Drogeham in Friesland. He was deposed in 1835 and became the most insistent voice among the Seceders for the full church order of Dort. When the new churches quarrelled in the 1830s and 1840s over whether to seek government recognition, over the wearing of clerical robes, and over how strictly the old church order should bind them, Van Velzen stood for order and confessional precision against Scholte's independency, and the disputes divided the movement. He served the Amsterdam congregation for many years and from 1854 was a teacher at the Theological School in Kampen, where he taught for many years. He was severe, and his severity cost the Secession unity it could have kept; but he was right that a church which recovers the doctrine of Dort without its government will lose both. His rule was Paul's: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines order in the church as regular government or discipline, and independency as the principle that every congregation is a complete church.
webster_full: OR'DER, n. Regular government; due subordination; regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things.
INDEPEND'ENCY, n. The principles or system of the Independents, who maintain that every congregation is a complete church, subject to no superior authority.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the execution of the laws by which the church is governed.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Phi 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
corruption_summary: The Seceder who insisted that Dort's doctrine needs Dort's church order.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation Van Velzen resisted is one every recovering church meets: to treat government as indifferent once the doctrine is right. The Seceders who wanted each congregation free to order itself soon found that they could not keep a common confession either. Paul joins doctrine and order in the same breath, “striving together for the faith of the gospel” (Phi 1:27).

The opposite failure is the one Van Velzen did not escape: precision that cannot tell a robe from a creed. The principle to recover is the apostle's balance, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21), which binds what Scripture binds and leaves free what it leaves free.
roots_summary: Greek euschemonos (G2156), decently; taxis (G5010), order; sunathleo (G4866), to strive together.
usage: “decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — his case for the church order of Dort.
“to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — the professor's polemic.
“hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — the measure for every dispute.

pos: n. (Albertus Christiaan van Raalte, 1811–1876, Seceder minister who led the Dutch emigration of 1846–47 and founded Holland, Michigan)
etymology: Latin Albertus, from Germanic adal, noble, and berht, bright; Dutch van Raalte, of Raalte in Overijssel.
biblical_def: Albertus van Raalte was refused ordination in the national church in 1835 because of his sympathy with the Secession, joined the Seceders, and was ordained by them. He served congregations in Overijssel through the years of fines and quartered soldiers and helped train ministers in his home. In the hungry 1840s, with the potato blight and continuing pressure on the Seceders, he became convinced that his people could only worship freely and live decently by emigrating. In the winter of 1846–47 he led the first party to the forests of western Michigan and founded the settlement of Holland, where the colonists cleared land, buried many of their children, and built a church before they built houses. Van Raalte was pastor, magistrate, land agent, and schoolmaster to the colony. In 1850 the Michigan churches joined the Reformed Church in America, a union that later divided them when the Christian Reformed Church separated in 1857, and he founded the academy that became Hope College. His people read their own journey in Abraham's: “he went out, not knowing whither he went” (Heb 11:8). Their hope was not Michigan: “now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines emigration as the removal of inhabitants from one country to another for the purpose of residence.
webster_full: EMIGRA'TION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
COL'ONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country to cultivate and inhabit it.
SET'TLEMENT, n. A colony newly established; a place or region newly planted.
scriptures: Heb 11:8
By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.
Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
Heb 11:9
By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: A Seceder pastor who led his flock across an ocean for liberty of worship.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation in the story is to tell it as an immigrant success, the founding of a prosperous town and a good college. The Seceders went for liberty of worship first and bread second, and they knew themselves pilgrims who were “dwelling in tabernacles” (Heb 11:9) wherever they settled.

The principle to recover is that a church may have to leave a nation to keep its confession, and that the Lord who called Abram, “Get thee out of thy country” (Gen 12:1), still calls. The 1857 division in Michigan over the Seceders' union with the eastern church is a second lesson: a union entered for comfort before confessional agreement is settled will not hold.
roots_summary: Greek exerchomai (G1831), to go out; paroikeo (G3939), to sojourn; Hebrew moledeth (H4138), kindred.
roots_lines: Greek exerchomai (G1831) — to go out, depart; Hebrews 11:8.
Greek paroikeo (G3939) — to sojourn, dwell as a stranger; Hebrews 11:9.
usage: “not knowing whither he went” (Heb 11:8) — the winter of 1846.
“dwelling in tabernacles” (Heb 11:9) — pilgrims in the Michigan woods.
“a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16) — the colony's true hope.

pos: n. (the Secession of 1834, in which confessional congregations withdrew from the Netherlands Reformed Church)
etymology: Dutch afscheiding, separation, from af, off, and scheiden, to divide.
biblical_def: The Afscheiding was the secession of confessional Reformed congregations from the Netherlands Reformed Church beginning at Ulrum in October 1834. Its causes were long-standing. In 1816 King William I gave the national church a new constitution from above, replacing its synodical government with boards responsible to the crown; the confessional subscription required of ministers had been loosened so that men could sign the Three Forms of Unity insofar as they agreed with Scripture; and an evangelical hymnbook of 1807 had been imposed alongside the psalms. When Hendrik de Cock was deposed, Hendrik Scholte, Anthony Brummelkamp, Simon van Velzen, Albertus van Raalte, and others followed him. The government invoked a Napoleonic law forbidding unauthorized gatherings of more than twenty persons: Seceder ministers were fined and jailed, services were broken up, and soldiers were billeted in members' homes. Toleration came gradually after 1840. The Seceders founded the Theological School at Kampen in 1854, sent thousands of emigrants to America, and in 1892 united with Kuyper's Doleantie churches. Their reproach was Christ's: “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seceder as one who withdraws from fellowship, applied specifically to a body that separated from the Church of Scotland.
webster_full: SECE'DER, n. One who secedes; one of a numerous sect of Presbyterians in Scotland, who seceded from the communion of the established church.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing; consent or attestation given by underwriting the name.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church.
scriptures: Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: The return of Dutch congregations to the confessions their national church had kept only on paper.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the corruption the Afscheiding answered as confessional nominalism: a church that keeps its standards in print while its government, its subscription formula, and its worship have abandoned them. The 1816 settlement put the crown in the place of the synod, and the loosened subscription put the minister in the place of the confession. Christ's indictment of the elders of His day fits it: “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).

The persecution that followed is a second lesson. A liberal state church that tolerated every opinion in its pulpits fined and jailed the people who held its own confession. Those who suffered it had the apostle's comfort: “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye” (1Pe 4:14). The modern reflex that treats secession as the sin and the apostate institution as the injured party reverses the moral order of 1834.
roots_summary: Greek exerchomai (G1831), to go forth; parembole (G3925), camp; oneidismos (G3680), reproach.
usage: “without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13) — the Seceders' place.
“come out from among them” (2Co 6:17) — the call they obeyed.
“happy are ye” (1Pe 4:14) — the blessing on the fined and jailed.

pos: n. (Lucas Lindeboom, 1845–1933, professor at Kampen, critic of Kuyper, and founder of Christian care for the mentally ill in the Netherlands)
etymology: Latin Lucas, from Greek Loukas, of Lucania; Dutch lindeboom, linden tree.
biblical_def: Lucas Lindeboom was a minister of the Seceder churches who became a professor at the Theological School at Kampen in 1883 and taught there for decades. He is remembered in two connections. In theology, he was the most persistent critic within the Reformed churches of Abraham Kuyper's system: he resisted the doctrine of presumptive regeneration, by which the children of the covenant were to be regarded as regenerate until they showed otherwise; he opposed Kuyper's teaching of justification from eternity; and after the union of 1892 he fought to keep Kampen as the churches' own school rather than see theological training absorbed into Kuyper's Free University. In mercy, he was the moving spirit behind the association founded in 1884 for the Christian care of the insane, which opened the first Reformed psychiatric institutions in the Netherlands at a time when the mentally ill were commonly confined in prisons and poorhouses. He believed that the church which confesses the doctrines of grace must show their fruit to the weakest: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an asylum as a place of refuge, and insanity as derangement of the intellect.
webster_full: ASY'LUM, n. A place of retreat and security; a refuge; an institution for the protection or relief of the unfortunate.
INSAN'ITY, n. The state of being unsound in mind; derangement of intellect; madness.
REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God are subdued.
scriptures: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: A Kampen professor who checked Kuyper's speculations and opened asylums for the insane.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error Lindeboom resisted was speculative: a theology that reasons from God's decree to conclusions Scripture does not draw, so that infants are presumed regenerate and the elect justified before they believe. His rule was the apostle's, “Prove all things” (1Th 5:21), and the Reformed churches eventually adopted the guarded Conclusions of Utrecht in 1905, which restrained the speculations he had opposed.

The second lesson is that orthodoxy and mercy are not alternatives. The man who would not yield an inch on justification spent decades building homes for the mentally ill, because “Pure religion and undefiled before God” (Jam 1:27) visits the afflicted. The modern habit of setting doctrinal precision against compassion has no purchase on his life.
roots_lines: Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to visit, look after; James 1:27.
usage: “one of the least of these my brethren” (Mat 25:40) — the asylums of 1884.
“Pure religion and undefiled” (Jam 1:27) — mercy joined to doctrine.
“Prove all things” (1Th 5:21) — his answer to Kuyper's speculations.

pos: n. (the Theological School of the Seceder churches at Kampen in Overijssel, opened 1854)
etymology: Dutch Kampen, the Hanseatic town on the IJssel; Latin seminarium, a seed-plot.
biblical_def: Kampen Seminary, the Theological School at Kampen, was opened in December 1854 by the Christian Seceded Reformed Church to train its ministers. Before that the Seceders had prepared men privately in the homes of pastors such as Van Velzen, Brummelkamp, and Van Raalte, with uneven results and much strife between the different schools. The synod of 1854 placed training under the churches themselves rather than a university, and called its first teachers from among the Secession's ministers, including Simon van Velzen and Helenius de Cock. Herman Bavinck taught dogmatics there from 1883 to 1902 and wrote the first edition of his Reformed Dogmatics at Kampen, and Klaas Schilder later taught there. After the union of 1892 the school remained the churches' seminary alongside Kuyper's Free University, a distinction Kampen's defenders thought essential: ministers of the church should be trained by the church and accountable to it. The principle is Paul's charge to Timothy, “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and the pattern of Ezra's Levites, who “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education, and theology as divinity, the science of God and divine things.
webster_full: SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.
THEOL'OGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things; or the science which teaches the existence, character and attributes of God.
SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council, either provincial or general.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: The church's own school, founded so that ministers would be trained by the body they serve.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The question Kampen answered is a live one: who trains the church's ministers? Where the answer is the university, the faculty answers to the academy and the church receives whatever the academy has made. The prophets placed the duty on the ministry itself: “the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7).

The principle to recover is that theological education is an act of the church, governed by its confession and accountable to its assemblies. Kampen's founders were poor men with no endowment, and they built the school because they would not hand their pulpits to teachers the churches could not discipline.
roots_summary: Greek didasko (G1321), to teach; Hebrew sekel (H7922), sense; bin (H995), to understand.
roots_lines: Hebrew parash (H6567) — to make distinct, declare; Nehemiah 8:8.
usage: “who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the reason for the school.
“gave the sense” (Neh 8:8) — exposition as the minister's craft.
“by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince” (Tit 1:9) — the aim of the curriculum.

pos: n. (the evangelical awakening of the early nineteenth century in Geneva, France, and the Netherlands)
etymology: French reveil, an awakening, from reveiller, to wake.
biblical_def: The Reveil was the evangelical awakening that ran through the Reformed churches of French-speaking Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands in the first half of the nineteenth century. In Geneva it began among theological students who met the Scottish layman Robert Haldane in 1816 and read Romans with him; out of that circle came Cesar Malan, Jean-Henri Merle d'Aubigne, Louis Gaussen, and Frederic Monod, who recovered the doctrines of grace and the inspiration of Scripture against the Socinian theology of the Genevan academy. In the Netherlands the movement was gentler and more aristocratic: the poet Willem Bilderdijk, his converted Jewish pupils Isaac da Costa and Abraham Capadose, Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer, and a circle of Amsterdam and Hague families who met for Bible study, founded Christian schools, and gave themselves to works of mercy among the poor and the prisoner. The Reveil prepared the ground for both the Secession of 1834 and the later revival under Kuyper, though most of its leaders stayed in the national church. It answered the prayer of the psalm: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revival in a religious sense as the renewal of piety and religious affections in a community.
webster_full: REVI'VAL, n. Renewed and more active attention to religion; an awakening of men to their spiritual concerns.
AWA'KENING, n. A revival of religion, or more general attention to religion, than usual.
PI'ETY, n. Piety in principle is a compound of veneration or reverence of the Supreme Being and love of his character.
scriptures: Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Eph 5:14
Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
corruption_summary: An awakening that recovered grace and Scripture in Geneva and the Netherlands, but too often stopped short of the church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What the Reveil recovered was real: the gospel as “the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Rom 1:16), and Scripture as inspired, against a rationalist clergy. Its weakness was its own: a piety of drawing rooms and conventicles that was often content to leave the church's confession, government, and pulpits in unbelieving hands.

The principle to recover is that revival must reach the church as well as the soul. The Seceders who left the national church in 1834 and the Reveil families who stayed in it loved the same Christ, but only one of them tried to obey the call of Eph 5:14 at the level of the institution: “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead” (Eph 5:14).
roots_summary: Hebrew chayah (H2421), to revive; samach (H8055), to rejoice; Greek egeiro (G1453), to awake.
usage: “Wilt thou not revive us again” (Psa 85:6) — the prayer of the Reveil.
“I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ” (Rom 1:16) — Haldane's Romans in Geneva.
“to revive the spirit of the humble” (Isa 57:15) — awakening as God's work.

pos: n. (Willem Bilderdijk, 1756–1831, Dutch poet and jurist, counter-revolutionary teacher of Da Costa and Groen van Prinsterer)
etymology: Dutch Willem, from Germanic wil, will, and helm, helmet; Bilderdijk, a place-name, dike of the Bilder.
biblical_def: Willem Bilderdijk was the most prolific Dutch poet of his age, a lawyer, linguist, and historian, and a man of violent opinions and irregular life. A loyal Orangist, he went into exile when the French-backed Patriots and then the Batavian Republic overthrew the old order in 1795, and returned to a Netherlands remade by the Revolution. From 1817 until 1827 he lectured privately at Leiden on Dutch history, and to a small circle of students, among them Isaac da Costa and Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer, he taught that the Revolution was not progress but rebellion against God, that the principles of 1789 — the sovereignty of the people, the rights of man without God — were the spirit of apostasy in political form, and that the old Calvinist Netherlands had been built on a better foundation. His own faith was a passionate supernaturalism more than a confessional Calvinism, and his private life was not what he preached. But his students carried his critique into the Reveil, the Anti-Revolutionary Party, and the Christian schools. He read the age through Psa 2:2: “The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD” (Psa 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revolution in politics as a material or entire change in the constitution of government.
webster_full: REVOLU'TION, n. In politics, a material or entire change in the constitution of government.
REBEL'LION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance.
PO'ET, n. The author of a poem; the inventor or maker of a metrical composition.

Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: The poet who taught a generation that the Revolution was apostasy, not progress.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the corruption Bilderdijk diagnosed as the revolutionary principle: the claim that political authority rises from the will of the people rather than from God, and that liberty means the rights of man against every given order. Scripture's counsel to the nation is the opposite: “fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21).

The honest caveat belongs in the same entry. Bilderdijk's nostalgia for the old order and his romantic temperament sometimes made tradition itself the standard, and his conduct contradicted his preaching. The principle to recover is the one his students refined: not the past for its own sake but the old paths of Jer 6:16 because they are God's, and the question of Psa 11:3 asked in earnest, “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3).

pos: n. (Isaac da Costa, 1798–1860, Amsterdam poet of Portuguese-Jewish birth, convert, and leader of the Dutch Reveil)
etymology: Hebrew Yitschaq, he laughs; Portuguese da Costa, of the coast.
biblical_def: Isaac da Costa was born into a distinguished Sephardic Jewish family of Amsterdam, studied law and letters at Leiden, and there came under the teaching of Willem Bilderdijk. In 1822 he and his friend Abraham Capadose were baptized as Christians. The next year he published Objections to the Spirit of the Age, a short book that attacked the cherished assumptions of liberal Holland — popular sovereignty, the cult of progress, smallpox vaccination, and above all the rationalism of the church — and that made him for a time the most hated writer in the country. He became the leading figure of the Reveil in Amsterdam, a poet of national stature, a lay preacher and Bible teacher, and in later life a teacher at the seminary of the Scottish Free Church mission in Amsterdam. He wrote much on the Jews and on the hope of Israel's conversion, and his own life was a sign of it: a son of Abraham who confessed Jesus as Messiah. He held with Paul that God has not cast away His people, and that “so all Israel shall be saved” (Rom 11:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a proselyte as a new convert to some religion, and conversion as a change of heart.
webster_full: CONVER'SION, n. In theology, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God and his law is subdued.
PROS'ELYTE, n. A new convert to some religion or religious sect, or to some particular opinion, system or party.
JEW, n. A Hebrew or Israelite.
scriptures: And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob:
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
corruption_summary: A converted Jew who told liberal Holland that the spirit of the age was not the Spirit of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Da Costa's Objections was a deliberate provocation against a culture that took its own assumptions for the conclusions of reason. Some of his targets were wrongly chosen, and his tone was needlessly contemptuous. But his central charge stands: an age that worships its own progress has made itself an idol, and the Christian is commanded, “be not conformed to this world” (Rom 12:2).

The principle to recover is the gospel's order, “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom 1:16). The modern reflex that treats Jewish conversion to Christ as an offence against Jewish identity would have puzzled a man who found in Jesus the fulfilment of everything Moses and the prophets had promised his fathers.
